briefs.headline: Govt working to resolve Scotch issue: Commerce secretary
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Dismissing suggestions that India was reneging on concessions given on Scotch whisky under the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) with the UK, commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal on Monday said the problem pertained to the classification of the product and govt was trying to find a solution to the tariff dispute at the earliest.
As reported by TOI on Saturday, Agrawal pointed out the issue revolved around court orders issued in 1991 and 2014, which mandated the import of Scotch under a category different from the one considered by govt while lowering the tariff under the India-UK CETA.
The commerce secretary said the understanding was that bulk Scotch whisky was imported only under HSN code 220830, and the duty concession was given accordingly. Govt was, however, subsequently informed that it was also being imported under HSN code 220890, meant for 'other' products, following legal pronouncements. These two tariff lines have different levels of concessions. Agrawal said trade negotiators on both sides were unaware of the court cases.
"We are working with the finance ministry to find a technical solution. Finding a technical solution also requires that we don't go against the court orders as such, but definitely the concessions under CETA also are to be equally respected," Agrawal said.

briefs.headline: IDBI not govt bank: SC; staff interest protected: Centre
briefs.bodyText:
New Delhi: The 
Supreme Court
 has held that IDBI is not a "State" within Article 12 of Constitution, which means it was not a govt entity, dealing a blow to the the bank's officer's association, even as govt maintained that the interests of employees and pensioners of the bank have been fully protected.
Last week, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran dismissed an appeal filed against a 2022 decision of the Bombay High Court, which struck down demand of the association, that called for retirement and provident fund benefits for employees of United Western Bank, which had merged with IDBI, arguing that the Centre retained administrative, functional and financial control over IDBI till 2018 and LIC, which acquired stake in the bank, was also owned and controlled by govt.
The SC ruling will also have an implication on the "strategic restructuring" of 
IDBI Bank
, where govt and LIC are selling over 60% stake held by in the bank to Fairfax. Employees have called for scrapping the sale, questioning the valuation and arguing that benchmarking it to public sector stock was not proper as IDBI is a private bank. Govt has also allayed concerns over retirement and salary benefits.
When contacted, DIPAM secretary Arunish Chawla said: "Govt and LIC are not employers under the Labour Code. 
IDBI Bank is the employer under the Code. A strategic transaction is executed through a share purchase agreement within the framework of the Contract Law. DIPAM appoints transaction and legal advisers, who in turn consult with the qualified parties on the one hand and with the bank management on the other. IDBI is a board-run banking company and management consults the employees internally, and has in this case presented a very robust protection framework for employees and pensioners, which is the best ever granted in such transactions.
 The service conditions of existing employees cannot be changed, modified or altered to their disadvantage after the strategic restructuring. The IDBI management has made sure all the service rules framed by the board are included in the annexures to the draft agreement. The pensioners are also fully protected, there is a special fund for it and their pension benefits will be full honoured."
Asked about the controversy over valuation of two properties, Chawla said Cuffe Parade headquarters in Mumbai was on 60-year lease and valuation was based on the rental saving for the remaining 25 years of lease. In the case of the training centre in Hyderabad, the property cannot be transferred in the open market and comparing its value to market-auctioned property would have been "absurd".

briefs.headline: Chaudhry's new high as CrowdStrike buys Zscaler
briefs.deck: $43Bn Deal Puts Serial Tech Entrepreneur From Himachal Pradesh In Global Spotlight
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Even as the cybersecurity industry witnesses a mega-deal, with CrowdStrike acquiring Zscaler in a $43 billion transaction, the story of Zscaler founder and serial tech entrepreneur Jay Chaudhry is a reminder of how extraordinary dreams can take root in the most unlikely places - even on a farm.
Born into a family of small farmers in a tiny village in the foothills of the Himalayas, on the Punjab-Himachal Pradesh border, about 30 km from the Bhakra Nangal dam, Chaudhry grew up with few of the amenities that urban India took for granted. "Our village got electricity when I finished 8th grade, running water when I finished 10th grade. I sat in a car for the first time after 12th grade. And I had a flight for the first time when I went to America to do my Master's," he told TOI in an interview in 2020.
His parents encouraged him to study because they had not had the opportunity themselves. His father had dropped out after Class 5 because the nearest middle school was too far away to walk to.
Chaudhry was academically gifted, and his teachers took an interest in him. He recalls one teacher in Class 10 telling him: "You're wasting your time in the class. Go and sit in those bushes and read. Come back, do your assignments and show me your assignments twice a day."
For pre-university (Class 11), he joined a college at the district headquarters, about 12 km away, a distance he would cover by bicycle. He went on to become a gold medallist at Himachal University. He initially considered studying engineering at Punjab Engineering College, but a teacher told him about the IITs and their system of admitting top performers from universities.
"I didn't even know about the IITs then," Chaudhry said. He applied for electronics engineering and secured admission to IIT-BHU. Moving from a village in Himachal Pradesh to the metropolitan environment of BHU was a cultural shock, but he adapted. With many students talking about pursuing higher studies in the US, he too applied during his final year.
The University of Cincinnati, Ohio, offered him a tuition scholarship. A Tata scholarship programme for students going abroad helped him fund his airline ticket. "It was just luck and it comes together sometimes," he said modestly.
Chaudhry earned a master's degree in computer engineering and another in industrial engineering from the University of Cincinnati, where he also met his wife, Jyoti, an MBA graduate from IIM Calcutta. He later worked at IBM and a few other companies before deciding to strike out on his own.
The internet boom of the 1990s had spawned a wave of successful startups, and Chaudhry wanted to build a company in internet security. But finding funding proved difficult. One day, Jyoti confronted him: "Hey, you keep talking about it (starting a venture). Either you do something or you shut up."
Chaudhry told her that the only way to get started was to put their life savings into the venture. Jyoti brought a combination of technology and finance expertise to the table. The two decided to take the risk and jointly founded SecureIT in 1996.
"It was probably the biggest and best gamble of our lives," he says.
Within two years, SecureIT was acquired by VeriSign for $70 million. The Atlanta-based venture became a success story, with 70 of its 80 employees becoming millionaires overnight.

briefs.headline: I-T Dept busts Rs 2,700 crore Chinese-linked gaming network; finds Rs 6.2 crore crypto
briefs.deck: The operation, conducted in the third week of October, led to the seizure of undeclared cryptocurrency valued at $650,000 (around Rs 6.2 crore). Investigators also detected two undisclosed properties in Dubai, for which approximately Rs 10 crore was reportedly paid in cryptocurrency. Tax officials have traced cryptocurrency transfers to overseas destinations and identified the ultimate…
briefs.bodyText:
The 
Income Tax Department
 has unearthed a payment network worth Rs 2,700 crore that was allegedly used by Chinese-controlled online gaming and betting platforms to collect money from Indian players.
The transactions were reportedly routed through an India-based payment intermediary and a web of shell companies that purported to operate digital-art businesses.
The operation, conducted in the third week of October, led to the seizure of undeclared cryptocurrency valued at $650,000 (around Rs 6.2 crore). Investigators also detected two undisclosed properties in Dubai, for which approximately Rs 10 crore was reportedly paid in cryptocurrency, people familiar with the probe told ET.
Decoding the network
Tax officials have traced cryptocurrency transfers to overseas destinations and identified the ultimate beneficiaries behind the network of shell companies, they said.
The investigation centres on 1stPe, an alleged front operating as a digital-art platform, and its promoters.
An initial examination of its server data indicated that the platform facilitated collections of about Rs 2,700 crore for Chinese gaming applications over a 40-month period, from July 2023 to October 2026. 
It allegedly earned around Rs 170 crore in commissions from these transactions.
The arrangement was allegedly structured to allow Indian users to make payments through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) to gaming applications linked to Chinese entities that could not accept such payments directly.
To enable the transactions, the gaming platforms’ servers had been whitelisted to connect with 1stPe, which functioned as the domestic payment intermediary.
Investigators have traced the flow of money through a payment gateway, with associates of 1stPe’s promoters allegedly establishing shell companies to handle the transactions.
These companies reportedly set up dummy websites displaying digital-art products and obtained Merchant IDs (MIDs) from an Indian payment intermediary by claiming to be legitimate businesses selling digital art.
The process began when a player deposited money into a gaming application using UPI. The payment request first reached 1stPe and was then passed to the payment intermediary using the MID of one of the shell companies. Airpay treated the transaction as a digital-art purchase and credited the money to the corresponding company’s bank account. Meanwhile, 1stPe charged a commission on each collection, earning a total of around Rs 170 crore, the financial daily reported.
The probe found that the companies were not engaged in genuine digital-art businesses and allegedly served as channels for collecting deposits from gaming users.
To avoid an unusually high concentration of transactions in individual accounts, the collections were distributed among multiple entities. When a bank or payment intermediary froze an account, the payment flow was allegedly redirected to another company.
The network reportedly created additional companies to keep the transactions running, using nominee directors, virtual offices and dummy websites to secure new merchant IDs.
An examination of server records revealed 113 client logins associated with Chinese gaming applications.
The Income Tax Department is investigating whether 1stPe functioned as an unlicensed payment aggregator. It is also tracing the ultimate recipients of the money and examining how the funds were moved overseas.

stories.headline: USA joint bid and UK confirmed as 2031 and 2035 FIFA Women's World Cup hosts
stories.deck: The USA in partnership with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will host in 2031, when the tournament will feature 48 teams for the first time
stories.bodyText:
FIFA on Monday (November 23, 2026) confirmed that a joint bid led by the United States will host the expanded, 48-team Women's World Cup in 2031, while the United Kingdom will host the following edition in 2035.
The winning bids were waved through by acclamation after FIFA president Gianni Infantino confirmed the USA, in partnership with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, was the "sole candidacy" to host in 2031, when the tournament will feature 48 teams for the first time.
The joint English, Scottish, Northern Irish and Welsh bid was also the only candidacy for 2035.
Infantino had already revealed last year that the respective bids for 2031 and 2035 were unchallenged and therefore set to be awarded the tournaments, with both being officially rubber-stamped at a virtual gathering of FIFA's member associations.
"As of 2031 there will be 48 teams and four hosts," said Infantino. "This is an incredible growth in just a few years."
The next Women's World Cup will take place next year in Brazil, running from June 24 to July 25. It will feature 32 teams, with the final at the Maracana Stadium in Rio de Janeiro.
Spain go into that tournament as the holders after winning the last Women's World Cup held in Australia and New Zealand in 2023, when they defeated current European champions England in the final.
The U.S. co-hosted this year's men's World Cup, with the majority of matches being played on American soil, including the final at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey which was won by Spain. That was the first men's edition featuring 48 teams.
The USA has hosted the Women's World Cup twice before, in 1999 and 2003, and is also the most successful nation in the tournament's history, having lifted the trophy four times.
'Landmark moment'
U.S. Soccer reacted to the announcement by saying the awarding of the 2031 tournament gave the country the chance to "build on the momentum" of this year's World Cup as well as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The United States are the reigning Olympic women's football champions.
No senior men's or women's World Cup has been played in the UK since England hosted and won the men's edition in 1966.
A joint statement by the four UK national associations described the announcement as "a landmark moment".
It is not yet known which cities will host matches at the respective tournaments, but most matches in 2031 are likely to take place in the United States while England can expect to have the lion's share of venues in 2035.
The UK bid proposed 22 stadiums in total, with 16 in England, three in Wales, two in Scotland and one in Northern Ireland.
Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said the two venues in the country would be the 52,000-seat Hampden Park in Glasgow as well as Hibernian's 20,000-seat Easter Road home in Edinburgh.
The draw for the 2027 Women's World Cup will take place on Friday, December 11, in Rio de Janeiro. The USA and England are among the nations aiming to secure qualification for the finals before then.
Infantino said Monday's Congress was organised "to celebrate women's football" and was "dedicated exclusively to that".
He therefore did not address his bid for re-election as the head of world football's governing body.
The election will take place at the next FIFA Congress to be held in the Moroccan capital Rabat in March, with France's Philippe Diallo and Japan's Kozo Tashima standing against the incumbent.

stories.headline: 2nd Test: Mitchell hopes Hagley pitch favours bowlers, says NZ were happy with draw
stories.deck: Daryl Mitchell is gearing up for a tougher battle in the second Test against India at Hagley Oval. He observed that the pitch might provide more bounce and bowler-friendly conditions. Following a stalemate in the first Test, he highlighted that both sides can take away valuable insights. With ample recovery time for the New Zealand bowlers, Mitchell is confident that the team is well-acquainted…
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: After a frustrating stalemate at the Basin Reserve, where only 24 wickets fell across five days and the pitch gradually became slower and lower, New Zealand all-rounder 
Daryl Mitchell
 is expecting a more competitive contest between bat and ball at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. Mitchell believes the surface for the second Test against India, starting Friday, could offer more bounce and give the bowlers a better chance of making an impact.
The first Test ended in a draw after New Zealand fought hard to deny India a victory on the final day. Mitchell, who remained unbeaten on 49, acknowledged that the Basin Reserve surface had not behaved as expected despite its generous covering of grass at the start.
"I think the nature of the base and surface at Basin Reserve is such that it usually looks pretty green at the start. We probably didn't expect it to get that slow and low over the course of five days, but now we're here at Hagley and I'm sure there might be a bit of bounce in this one," Mitchell said.
'We were both pretty happy to do so': Mitchell on final-day draw
India threw everything at New Zealand on the final day, pushing for a victory before the two sides eventually agreed to shake hands with around an hour of play remaining. 
Mitchell admitted that the Black Caps were equally relieved to settle for a draw after a demanding five days, particularly given the workload on the bowlers.
"Look, you could see the amount of effort they were putting in throughout the day. It takes a toll on the bowlers' bodies, and it's a big series as well. When they wanted to shake hands, we were both pretty happy to do so," Mitchell said.
The 35-year-old also credited New Zealand's collective character for standing firm and batting out the final day to frustrate India.
"I think it's just the character of the group to keep fighting as much as we can and keep giving to that Black Cap. That's sort of what we pride ourselves on, and it's nice to show it again," he said.
Familiar Hagley Oval offers New Zealand confidence
Mitchell will be particularly pleased to return to Christchurch, where he has played extensively over the years. The all-rounder believes familiarity with the venue and its conditions will help New Zealand prepare for the second Test.
"Yeah, it's cool to be home and to wake up in your own bed. The morning of Test matches is always nice, looking forward to it."
"A number of us have played a lot of cricket at Hagley Oval over the last decade or so, so we know what conditions to expect. It's a beautiful ground to play Test cricket at, and we're all looking forward to it," Mitchell said.
While the drawn opener provided positives for both sides, Mitchell acknowledged that New Zealand's bowlers needed time to recover before the next challenge.
"Both teams will take a lot of positives out of that Test match. For us, it's our first hit-out in Test cricket for a while. I know the bowlers were probably a bit sore a few days ago, but they've got a few days' rest now to get ready to go again. So, yeah, look, it's only going to help us going forward," he added.

stories.headline: Pakistan defeat sparks major shake-up: Tilak Varma makes three changes to India A XI
stories.deck: India A made three changes to their playing XI in preparation for the Asia Cup match against the UAE. The changes come after their recent defeat to Pakistan A, where they struggled to chase a target. UAE captain Basil Hameed won the toss and opted to bat first in Doha. India A needs to win this match to secure a spot in the semifinals.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India A captain 
Tilak Varma
 made three changes to the playing XI for their crucial Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 Group B match against the United Arab Emirates in Doha on Tuesday.
UAE captain Basil Hameed won the toss and elected to bat at the University of Doha for Science and Technology.
India brought in Prabhsimran Singh, Harsh Dubey and Arshad Khan in place of Ayush Badoni, Vipraj Nigam and Prince Yadav.
Asia Cup Rising Stars: Badoni, Nigam, Prince dropped after Pakistan defeat
The changes came after India A suffered a 48-run defeat against Pakistan A in their previous match on Sunday.
India had bowled Pakistan out for 313 in 49.2 overs but failed to chase down the target. Badoni and Vipraj both had disappointing outings with the bat, getting out for ducks.
However, Vipraj did contribute with the ball, taking two wickets for 46 runs in his eight overs. Prince Yadav also picked up two wickets but conceded 60 runs in 9.2 overs.
India will now look for a stronger all-round performance against the UAE.
Asia Cup Rising Stars: India A's semifinal hopes at stake
The defeat against Pakistan has put pressure on India's semifinal hopes, but they remain in contention for a place in the last four.
India A have two points from two matches and need a win against the UAE to reach four points and secure qualification.
Pakistan A have already booked their semifinal spot after winning both their group matches. 
The top two teams from Group B will advance to the semifinals, scheduled for November 26 and 27.
Asia Cup Rising Stars: Where do India A stand in the points table?
Pakistan A are at the top of Group B with four points from two matches. India A and Nepal have two points each, while the UAE are yet to open their account.
Nepal kept their qualification hopes alive with a six-wicket win over the UAE on Sunday. Pakistan A then defeated India A to seal their place in the semifinals.
India's positive net run rate of +2.580 gives them an advantage over Nepal and could prove important if the teams finish level on points.
How can India A qualify for the semifinals?
India A have several possible routes to the last four, with their match against the UAE playing a key role.
1. India A beat UAE and Pakistan A beat Nepal
This is the simplest route. A win will take India A to four points and guarantee them a semifinal spot, regardless of the result of the other match.
2. India A beat UAE and Nepal beat Pakistan A
In this situation, India A, Pakistan A and Nepal will all finish with four points. Net run rate will decide the final standings.
India A will have an advantage because of their 306-run win over Nepal earlier in the tournament. Their current net run rate of +2.580 is much better than Nepal's -2.461.
3. India A's match against UAE is washed out and Pakistan A beat Nepal
A washout will give India A one point, taking their tally to three. They will still qualify if Pakistan A beat Nepal, as Nepal will remain on two points.
4. UAE beat India A and Pakistan A beat Nepal
A defeat will make India's task difficult but will not end their campaign immediately.
Pakistan A will finish with six points, while India A, Nepal and the UAE will all have two points. Net run rate will then decide the second semifinal spot. India's current advantage over Nepal could prove crucial, but the margin of defeat against the UAE will matter.
5. UAE beat India A and Nepal beat Pakistan A
This is the combination that will knock India A out. Nepal and Pakistan A will finish with four points each and qualify for the semifinals, while India A will remain on two points.

briefs.headline: Priyansh Arya rewrites SMAT record books with 181, hits 19 sixes
briefs.deck: Arya turned the PowerPlay into a personal exhibition of six-hitting, taking 22 runs apiece off pacer R. Silambarasan and left-arm spinner Sai Kishore in successive overs
briefs.bodyText:
Delhi skipper Priyansh Arya rewrote the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy (SMAT) record books with a breathtaking 68-ball 181 (7x4, 19x6) against Tamil Nadu in a Group-B clash at the Daly College ground in Indore on Tuesday (November 24, 2026), registering the highest individual score and hitting the most sixes in an innings in the tournament’s history. It is also the highest T20 score by an Indian.
He went past Tilak Varma’s previous best of 151 with a six over long-on off Sai Kishore, moving from 149 to 155. On the next ball, he equalled Punit Bisht’s record of 17 sixes in an innings with a hit over deep square leg. He later claimed the record outright, sending his 18th six over deep cover off a full toss from Gurjapneet Singh.
Arya turned the PowerPlay into a personal exhibition of six-hitting, taking 22 runs apiece off pacer R. Silambarasan and left-arm spinner Sai Kishore in successive overs (fourth and fifth).
He began by launching Silambarasan over deep extra cover and deep midwicket for consecutive sixes, followed by a four over the infield to deep extra cover and an upper cut over deep backward point for another maximum.
Sai Kishore fared no better, as Arya first cleared the ropes straight down the ground before bringing up his half-century off just 18 balls with a slog sweep over deep backward square leg. A full toss was dispatched to deep backward square leg for four, and a six over long-on completed another 22-run over.
He continued the onslaught against Shahrukh Khan in the final over of the PowerPlay, slog-sweeping him over deep midwicket for six, cutting him through deep cover for four and finishing with another straight six.
Arya raced to 78 off just 26 balls as Delhi plundered 94 for one in the PowerPlay. He brought up his hundred off 36 balls with a straight six off Shahrukh. He was dropped on 148 off Silambarasan by Amith Sathvik at long-off.
Delhi finished with 275/5 in 20 overs.

briefs.headline: Priyansh Arya rewrites history, breaks KL Rahul's record for highest T20 score
briefs.deck: Priyansh Arya, the captain of Delhi, delivered an extraordinary performance in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy by scoring 181 runs. His remarkable innings featured an incredible 19 sixes, breaking KL Rahul's previous record for a T20 innings. Delhi finished strong, amassing a total of 275 runs for five wickets, moving Arya to second place in the highest individual scores of men's T20 cricket, marking…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Delhi captain Priyansh Arya produced a breathtaking batting display on Tuesday, smashing a sensational 181 off just 68 balls against Tamil Nadu in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy to rewrite the T20 record books. He became the highest-scoring Indian batter in T20 cricket history, surpassing 
KL Rahul
's previous record, while also equalling the world record for the most sixes in a single T20 innings.
The left-handed opener smashed an astonishing 19 sixes and 7 fours to power Delhi to a mammoth 275/5 in their 20 overs at the Daly College Ground in Indore. His 181 is now the second-highest individual score in men's T20 cricket, behind South African Lhuan-dre Pretorius, who scored an unbeaten 188 off 79 balls for Titans against Knights in the CSA Pro20 Cup in October 2026.
Arya's innings eclipsed Rahul's 152 not out, scored earlier this year for Delhi Capitals against Punjab Kings in IPL 2026, to become the highest individual T20 score by an Indian.
36-ball hundred, 19 sixes: Arya goes on record-breaking rampage
Sent in to bat by Tamil Nadu, Delhi suffered an early setback when Yash Dhull departed for eight in the third over. However, Arya ensured that the early wicket did little to derail Delhi's innings as he took the attack to the opposition bowlers.
He found some support from Nitish Rana, with the duo adding 118 runs for the second wicket. Rana contributed 18 off 17 deliveries, but Arya did most of the damage at the other end.
The Delhi captain raced to his hundred in just 36 deliveries, hammering 12 sixes and four boundaries in the process. He continued his assault after reaching the milestone, going past Rahul's Indian record of 152 not out before eventually falling for a remarkable 181 off 68 balls.
His 19 sixes took him level with Finn Allen's record, set in June 2025, while putting him past Chris Gayle and Estonia's Sahil Chauhan, who had smashed 18 sixes each. Arya now shares the record for the most sixes hit by a batter in a single T20 innings.
Arya's 181 takes Delhi to 275/5
Arya's extraordinary knock provided the foundation for Delhi's imposing total of 275/5 in 20 overs. The next-best contribution came from Anuj Rawat, who remained unbeaten on 29, underlining just how much of Delhi's scoring was driven by their captain.
Highest individual scores in T20 cricket
- Lhuan-dre Pretorius - 188* (79)
- Priyansh Arya       - 181 (68)
- Chris Gayle         - 175* (66)
- Aaron Finch         - 172 (76)
- Hamza Khan          - 164* (65)
Rahul's previous Indian record had come in spectacular circumstances as well. His unbeaten 152 for Delhi Capitals against Punjab Kings in Delhi earlier in IPL 2026 featured 16 fours and nine sixes, helping DC post 264/2. However, the mammoth total was not enough to secure victory, with Punjab Kings chasing it down with seven balls to spare.
Interestingly, Arya was on the opposite side of that contest and played a significant role in the successful chase, smashing 43 off just 17 balls. He added 126 for the opening wicket with Prabhsimran Singh, who top-scored with 76 off 26 deliveries, as Punjab completed a remarkable chase.
On Tuesday, however, Arya ensured that his name would stand above Rahul's in the Indian T20 record books, producing an innings that also rewrote the global six-hitting record.

briefs.headline: Shubman Gill reveals why Team India cancelled planned activity
briefs.deck: India's cricket team faced a challenging Test match against New Zealand, requiring their bowlers to deliver extensive overs. Captain Shubman Gill acknowledged the bowlers' efforts and canceled planned team activities to provide them with a break. He emphasized the need for ICC to lift the ban on using saliva to maintain the ball's condition. Gill pointed out that a softer ball makes it harder for…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India's bowlers had to put in a long shift during the drawn first Test against New Zealand in Wellington. With the attack delivering close to 250 overs across the two innings, the team management decided to cancel a planned team activity in Christchurch.
India captain 
Shubman Gill
 said the players deserved a break after such a demanding effort. He also promised that the bowlers would be taken out for dinner.
"Our bowlers have put in so many overs, we will definitely take them (out for a dinner). We had a team activity but after bowling so many overs it stands cancelled," Gill said.
Bowlers deliver close to 250 overs
The Indian bowling attack had a busy Test match, with the bowlers delivering 121 overs in New Zealand's first innings and another 120 in the second.
Jasprit Bumrah bowled 49 overs across the two innings and picked up five wickets. Akash Deep bowled 43 overs and took three wickets, while Anshul Kamboj delivered 45 overs and claimed three wickets.
Prasidh Krishna bowled 45 overs and took three wickets. Washington Sundar also put in a long shift, bowling 55 overs and picking up one wicket.
Gill said India had started the final day well but could not make the most of their opportunities.
"We were very good in first session, were looking to get into the tail. Got two half chances and maybe could have been different. Energy was good and everyone was enjoying," he said.
Gill wants ICC to review saliva ban
Gill also urged the ICC to reconsider its ban on using saliva to shine the ball. He said the Kookaburra ball was becoming soft too quickly, making it difficult for bowlers to take wickets on pitches offering little help.
New Zealand batted for 75 overs on the final day, scoring 120 runs for the loss of three wickets. They finished their second innings at 239 for five, and neither team could force a result.
"We are way past Covid times. There was a rule that you can't apply saliva to shine the ball. It's been 7-8 years now, I still don't understand why they are not allowing it," Gill said.
The India captain said the ball had lost its hardness early in the match.
"Our first ball, I think after 25-30 overs, the ball became very soft. I think they also complained," he said.
"We saw this in England as well. In the first 3-4 matches, we gave a slightly different ball in the Oval,"
Soft ball makes life difficult for bowlers
Gill also raised concerns about the quality of the Kookaburra ball. He said a softer ball makes it harder for fielders to take catches behind the wicket, especially when the pitch does not offer much movement.
"I don't know if the quality of the balls has come down or what happened. But in such conditions, if there is no help from the wicket, and the ball also becomes soft, then it becomes very difficult for the bowlers to take wickets," he said.
"They don't carry the edges. So, the caught-behind dismissal becomes harder. If there is not so much movement in the pitch, then the LBW remains on hold."
Gill felt allowing saliva would help teams maintain the ball's condition for a longer period, particularly on flat pitches.
"And on the saliva, yes, I do believe that teams should be allowed to use saliva. It was a rule that was made effective during COVID. I think we are long past that," he said.
"The condition of the ball, if you're not shining the ball or if you're not able to maintain the ball well, especially on wickets like these, it makes the job of the bowlers very difficult."
He said India had faced a similar problem during their 2025 tour of England, where the ball became soft early in the innings.
"Ideally, we understand after 50 overs, the ball obviously will go soft. But if the ball is going soft after 25-30 overs or it's going out of shape and you're also not able to maintain the ball and use saliva, then it's a very difficult job for the bowlers," he said.

briefs.headline: Gukesh vs Sindarov, World Chess C'ship: Past is past, the board is set, it starts now
briefs.deck: It’s a completely different match, opponent and venue, says title-holder Gukesh as he squares up against challenger Sindarov in a battle of twenty-year-olds.
briefs.bodyText:
The ability to play fluid, sharp, playable positions with elan, avoiding oversight and the crucial aspect of time management are all expected to play a decisive role in the World Chess Championship match between D Gukesh and challenger Javokhir Sindarov.
The 14-game Classical match, with provision of tiebreaks in faster time control, will start in Geneva, Switzerland, on Tuesday.
The defending champion Gukesh has great ability to calculate, surprise and corner opponents over the board to squeeze out tiny advantages even from most unlikely positions. And his fellow 20-year-old Sindarov’s strength in principled chess coupled with an aggressive-yet-practical approach and resilience have taken him thus far.
To be able to set the ego aside and offer/accept a draw will also play a part. And we are yet to talk about their teams and the level of AI-backed, expertly curated and tailor-made lines through exhaustive opening preparation.
Gukesh had recalled a dinner with his mentor V Anand organised by chess.com a few months ago. “You will wake up having butterflies in your stomach. Going to the game itself is a big achievement. And then you have to push past your limits,” he remembers telling the master.
Anand pointed out that he could be assailed by a lack of proper sleep during the match. “And, constantly thinking about what could happen and how you deal with it,” the man who had been there, done that had added. The inner battle should be as fascinating as what would unfold on the squares.
For the first time in 99 years, there will be no live audience at the venue, with the exception, of course, of those who are working on site. The idea is that millions are expected to tune in to the live streaming that starts at 7.30pm IST.
Sindarov, who made this match by winning the 2025 knockout World Cup in Goa and round-robin Candidates meet in Cyprus, is not reading too much into his great form.
“My chances in this match are 50-50. I don’t want to say anything. The match will be very tough. Fourteen games... anything can happen,” he said.
Champions raise their game and move mountains when it matters. Gukesh had done that at least four times in the last five years — at the 2022 and 2024 Olympiads, the Candidates of 2024 and at the World Championship campaign against Ding Liren of China in the same year.
The contestants won’t be just reading events and cross-checking preferred playable opening lines while preparing, they will also be reading breathing patterns of the other before, during and after the games to get clues to arrive at precise evaluation of the position and situation.
In the heat of the battle, they won’t have the luxury of computerbacked evaluation bars to navigate through challenging situations.
A comparative study of the number of decisive games in the recent World Championship matches provides an interesting picture.
From 2010 to 2018, there were fourteen decisive results in 69 games spanning six matches. Just about 1/5th were decisive games. But after the Covid break — in three matches of 2021, 2023 and 2024 — there were 15 decisive results in 39 games. It showed that a more than 1/3rds decisive swing.
If the trend continues, we are in for a roller-coaster ride.
Gukesh told a press conference on Sunday: “Whatever happened till now just gets erased. It’s a completely different match, opponent and place. I’m feeling quite enthusiastic to test myself and see what I am capable of.”
And then he repeated what he has been saying for some time now: “I am not here to defend anything. I am here to win it all over again. That is my mindset.”

briefs.headline: The causes for Wellington draw and its impact on India’s WTC final chances
briefs.deck: If India win in Christchurch, only then can it hope to make it to the WTC final by winning four of the five Border Gavaskar Trophy matches against Australia early next year
briefs.bodyText:
Leeds 2025, Colombo (SSC) 2026 and Wellington 2026. Thrice in the last 18 months, India has entered Day 5 of an overseas Test match eyeing a rare Test win away from home. But on all three occasions, India couldn’t rise to the occasion and return with 12 points on offer for a win in the World Test Championship (WTC).
While Leeds saw Ben Duckett blowing India away that resulted in a disappointing loss for India, in Colombo or Wellington, the last day saw the opposition batters batting the day out to deprive India of a win.
No doubt, the pitch was a major factor at Basin Reserve, considering it didn’t offer any lateral movement and it went slower and lower than a majority of subcontinental decks on offer, not to mention it just did not crack down. Still, based on the proceedings in the New Zealand capital, here are the two mistakes and its ramification on another major factor:
The combination
The exclusion of Mohammed Siraj remained the talk of the town, even after the end of the match. Let’s not get into the unnecessary politicisation of India’s team selection for the first Test, but the fact remains that Siraj could have been more than a handful, especially with the ball on Day 4 and Day 5, with his workhorse-like work ethic.
Captain Shubman Gill obviously defended the decision, stating Siraj understood when he sat down with him prior to the game, adding that he doesn’t know whether he agreed with it or not. But the fact remains that, irrespective of whether the Indian team management admits or not, Siraj’s absence must have been felt, especially when it comes to running in at full steam and trying to put batters under pressure time and again, even in the most adverse conditions for pace bowlers.
With all the focus on Siraj, one cannot forget that Ravindra Jadeja’s experience and accuracy in such conditions could have also come in handy. Washington Sundar did try his best, but the fact that he remains more of a drifter than a turner and did not actually work out in India’s favour. Jadeja instead would have been extremely useful, especially when it comes to bogging the batters down with his stump-to-stump line.
Nevertheless, when this reporter asked Captain Gill pointedly whether the duo’s absence was felt, Gill stuck to his guns and responded with the shortest response of the post-match media conference in Wellington. “No, I don’t think so,” was his short reply and it thus indicated that India is bound to stick to the same combination in Christchurch for the last Test.
The strategy
Many may feel that having a go at India’s inability to pick 20 wickets on such a highway-like strip is unnecessary criticism. But the fact remains that India has time and again stated that it selected bowling combination that could fetch 20 wickets. And it doesn’t need a novice to remind that the key for winning a Test is to pick 20 wickets.
Besides selection, did India get its approach right on Day 5? Seldom did it look like it was desperately trying to exert pressure on batters. Even when Daryl Mitchell was trying to buy, rather waste, time with all sorts of antics that batters usually resort to while batting out for a draw. Not once did India show the urgency that is required for a fielding team desperate to go for the kill.
Perhaps more than strategy, it’s a question of approach as well. But the sooner India realise, the better it will be.
The impact on WTC equation
The impact of the Wellington draw in WTC table has been huge both for New Zealand and India. The draw has in a way adversely affected both New Zealand and India’s chances in the WTC table. Let’s not get too much into the New Zealand equation. India now finds itself in a virtually unlosable situation for the remaining six tests.
If India win in Christchurch, only then can it hope to make it to the WTC final by winning four of the five Border Gavaskar Trophy matches against Australia early next year. That too, with other results going its way.
Otherwise, a WTC final in Gautam Gambhir’s tenure as head coach will continue to remain a distant dream.
